entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 39 Jr 39:1-18 . Jerusalem Taken. Zedekiah's Fate. Jeremiah Cared for. Ebed-melech Assured. This chapter consists of two parts: the first describes the capture of Jerusalem, the removal of the people to Babylon, and the fate of Zedekiah, and that of Jeremiah. The second tells of the assurance of safety to Ebed-melech. 1. ninth year ... tenth month-- and on the tenth day of it ( Jr 52:4 ; 2Ki 25:1-4 ). From Jr 39:2 , "eleventh year ... fourth month ... ninth day," we know the siege lasted one and a half years, excepting the suspension of it caused by Pharaoh. Nebuchadnezzar was present in the beginning of the siege, but was at Riblah at its close ( Jr 39:3 , 6 ; compare Jr 38:17 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10452"/><div sID="gen18639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10452"/><hi type="bold">4. the king's garden--</hi>The "gate" to it from the upper, city above was appropriated to the kings alone; stairs" led down from Mount Zion and the palace to the king's garden below (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Ne 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen18639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">two walls--</hi>Zedekiah might have held the upper city longer, but want of provisions drove him to flee by the double wall south of Zion, towards the plains of Jericho (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jr 39:5</reference>), in order to escape beyond Jordan to Arabia-Deserta. He broke an opening in the wall to get out (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.12">Eze 12:12</reference>). <div eID="gen18640" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10454"/><div sID="gen18643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10454"/><hi type="bold">6. slew ... sons ... before his eyes--</hi>previous to his eyes being "put out" (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.7">Jr 39:7</reference>); literally, "dug out." The Assyrian sculptures depict the delight with which the kings struck out, often with their own hands, the eyes of captive princes. This passage reconciles <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">Jr 32:4</reference>, "his eyes shall behold his eyes"; with <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>, "he shall not see Babylon, though he shall die there."<div eID="gen18643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slew all ... nobles--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">Jr 27:20</reference>). <div eID="gen18644" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10455"/><div sID="gen18645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10455"/><hi type="bold">8. burned ... the houses--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jr 52:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">13</reference>). Not immediately after the taking of the city, but in the month after, namely, the fifth month (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.39.2">Jr 39:2</reference>). The delay was probably caused by the princes having to send to Riblah to know the king's pleasure as to the city. <div eID="gen18645" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10461"/><div sID="gen18653" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10461"/><hi type="bold">14. Gedaliah--</hi>son of Ahikam, the former supporter of Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jr 26:24</reference>). Gedaliah was the chief of the deserters to the Chaldeans, and was set over the remnant in Judea as one likely to remain faithful to Nebuchadnezzar. His residence was at Mizpah (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">Jr 40:5</reference>).<div eID="gen18653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">home--</hi>the house of Gedaliah, wherein Jeremiah might remain as in a safe asylum. As in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.1">Jr 40:1</reference> Jeremiah is represented as "bound in chains" when he came to Ramah among the captives to be carried to Babylon, this release of Jeremiah is thought by Maurer to be distinct from that in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">Jr 40:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.6">6</reference>. But he seems first to have been released from the court of the prison and to have been taken to Ramah, still in chains, and then committed in freedom to Gedaliah.<div eID="gen18654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelt among the people--</hi>that is, was made free. <div eID="gen18655" type="x-p"/>

Gedaliah was the chief of the deserters to the Chaldeans, and was set over the remnant in Judea as one likely to remain faithful to Nebuchadnezzar. His residence was at Mizpah ( Jr 40:5 ). home-- the house of Gedaliah, wherein Jeremiah might remain as in a safe asylum. As in Jr 40:1 Jeremiah is represented as "bound in chains" when he came to Ramah among the captives to be carried to Babylon, this release of Jeremiah is thought by Maurer to be distinct from that in Jr 40:5 , 6 . But he seems first to have been released from the court of the prison and to have been taken to Ramah, still in chains, and then committed in freedom to Gedaliah. dwelt among the people-- that is, was made free.
